location: Medina, Basra (the Battle of the Camel), Siffin on the upper Euphrates, al-Nahrawan near al-Mada'in, and Kufa

date.note: From the killing of the caliph Uthman in Medina in 35/656 to the killing of Ali in Kufa in Ramadan 40/January 661, after which Mu'awiya's authority was generally acknowledged, formally with al-Hasan ibn Ali's abdication in 41/661. The Battle of the Camel is dated 10 or 15 Jumada II 36/4 or 9 December 656; the main fighting at Siffin took place in 37/657; the Battle of al-Nahrawan is placed by al-Tabari under the year 37 and dated by many modern historians to 38/658. The reports give variant dates for Ali's death within Ramadan 40.

summary: The First Fitna was the first civil war within the Muslim community (35-40/656-661), opened by the killing of the caliph Uthman and fought during the caliphate of Ali ibn Abi Talib, through the Battle of the Camel, the Battle of Siffin and the ensuing arbitration, the secession of the Kharijites, and Ali's assassination, after which the Umayyad Mu'awiya became caliph. Later Sunni, Shi'i, and Kharijite/Ibadi communities each defined themselves in part through their judgments of its participants.
description: The war began with the killing of the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, in Medina in 35/656 by insurgents from Egypt, Kufa, and Basra who had pressed grievances against his governance and appointments. Ali ibn Abi Talib received allegiance (bay'a) in Medina amid that turmoil; his authority was not recognised by all. Three prominent figures, the Prophet's widow A'isha and the Companions Talha and al-Zubayr, left for Basra demanding retribution for Uthman's blood, and the reports differ over whether the latter two had given allegiance to Ali willingly, grudgingly, or not at all. Their forces met Ali's at the Battle of the Camel near Basra in Jumada II 36/December 656, named for the camel carrying A'isha's litter; Talha and al-Zubayr were killed and A'isha was escorted back to Medina. Ali then moved his base to Kufa. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the governor of Syria and Uthman's kinsman, withheld allegiance and demanded retribution for Uthman. The two armies met at Siffin on the upper Euphrates in 37/657, where the Companion Ammar ibn Yasir, fighting on Ali's side, was killed. According to the accounts collected by al-Tabari, when the Syrians, at the suggestion of Amr ibn al-As, raised copies of scripture on their lances as an appeal to the word of God, many of Ali's Iraqi supporters pressed him to stop fighting, and an agreement was drawn up for each side to appoint an arbitrator (hakam), Abu Musa al-Ash'ari for Ali and Amr ibn al-As for Mu'awiya. The reports of the arbitrators' later meeting (placed at Dumat al-Jandal or Adhruh) are, in the translator G. R. Hawting's words, 'confusing and obscure'; they are generally read as reaching no agreement accepted by both sides, while weakening Ali's standing. A body of Ali's own followers came to hold that submitting the dispute to human arbitration contradicted the principle that judgment belongs to God alone (la hukma illa li-llah); they demanded that Ali repent and seceded from him, and they are known as the Kharijites (khawarij, 'those who went out'). Ali defeated them at al-Nahrawan, with heavy loss of life among the seceders, while Mu'awiya extended his control over Egypt. In Ramadan 40/January 661 Ali was struck down in the mosque of Kufa by Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, a Kharijite who is reported to have sought vengeance for those killed at al-Nahrawan. Ali's son al-Hasan received allegiance in Kufa but reached an accommodation with Mu'awiya and abdicated in 41/661, a year later remembered in Sunni historiography as the 'year of unity' ('am al-jama'a); Mu'awiya's accession inaugurated the Umayyad dynasty. The fitna became a defining point of reference for later Muslim communities, which, in Hawting's formulation, expressed and defined their own identities through their attitudes toward its participants, a traditional picture that modern historians regard as simplified but formative. In Sunni tradition, as expressed in creeds such as that of al-Tahawi, the Companions on all sides are to be spoken of only with good; their conflict is commonly treated as a matter of independent judgment (ijtihad) in which the participants are not condemned, and believers are enjoined to refrain from judging or disparaging them, while Ali is counted as the legitimate fourth caliph. Many Sunni scholars further hold that Ali was in the right in these wars and that his opponents erred in their ijtihad without thereby ceasing to be Companions of standing; they cite among other evidence the prophetic report, transmitted in Sahih al-Bukhari, that Ammar would be killed by 'the rebellious party' (al-fi'a al-baghiya). In Shi'i tradition the fitna is read in light of the conviction that Ali was the Prophet's divinely designated successor and imam, so that those who fought him opposed rightful authority, a reading set out in modern Shi'i scholarship such as that of S. H. M. Jafri; Shi'i authors differ in how they assess individual participants such as A'isha, Talha, and al-Zubayr. The Kharijites held that judgment belongs to God alone and that Ali, by accepting arbitration, and his opponents, by their rebellion, had forfeited legitimate authority. Ibadi Muslims, whose tradition scholarship traces to the moderate wing of the early secession but who reject the name 'Kharijite', regard the people of al-Nahrawan as upright Muslims (a stance already argued in early Ibadi writings such as the epistle attributed to Salim ibn Dhakwan) who sought to preserve the just imamate, and hold that the first caliphs governed justly until, in their assessment, Uthman in his later years and Ali after the arbitration departed from it. Sunnis, Shi'is, and Ibadis thus share the broad narrative outline while differing sharply over the legitimacy and standing of its principal actors; this entry records each judgment as that community's own.
editorial_notes: This event entry is written under neutrality principles #1, #2, and #7 for one of the most sectarian-sensitive episodes in Islamic history. The narrative outline (the killing of Uthman, Ali's accession, the Camel, Siffin, the arbitration, the secession, al-Nahrawan, Ali's assassination, al-Hasan's abdication, Mu'awiya's accession) is given as the framework common to the Sunni, Shi'i, and Ibadi traditions and to modern historiography; every judgment about who acted rightly is attributed to a named community (Sunni restraint about the Companions and the ijtihad reading; the Shi'i conviction of Ali's designated imamate; the Kharijite principle of no judgment but God's; the Ibadi self-understanding and its rejection of the Kharijite label) and none is adopted in editorial voice. The Sunni position on the Companions is stated on its own terms, not as neutral fence-sitting, and the Shi'i position is stated as a theological conviction, not as a historical finding. Contested details (whether Talha and al-Zubayr gave allegiance willingly, grudgingly, or not at all, the place and outcome of the arbitrators' meeting, the date of al-Nahrawan, the exact day of Ali's death) are flagged as varying in the reports. The phrase 'am al-jama'a is identified as a Sunni historiographical usage. Ali's accession is described without calling it the first contested succession, since whether the earlier successions were contested is itself disputed between Sunni and Shi'i readings of Saqifa. The Sunni reading is given in both its forms, the general restraint about judging the Companions and the widely held view that Ali was in the right while his opponents erred in ijtihad; the hadith on Ammar is cited as the evidence Sunni scholars adduce, not as an editorial verdict on the war. The account of the raising of the scriptures and the arbitration follows al-Tabari as summarized by his translator; Hinds's study of the arbitration document is cited for the scholarly analysis of the agreement's text and dating, and Madelung for the overall reconstruction; Madelung is noted as a study that argues in favour of Ali's claim, cited as scholarship, not as endorsement. Sources triangulate three lenses per principles #8 and #9: Western academic scholarship (Madelung; Hinds), the classical primary chronicle (al-Tabari, SUNY vols. 16 and 17, drawing on Abu Mikhnaf and other early transmitters), and modern Muslim scholarship from more than one vantage (Ayoub, presenting Sunni and Shi'i perspectives; Afsaruddin, on Sunni memory of the Companions), with the Shi'i voice represented by Jafri and the Ibadi voice by Hoffman's study of Ibadi doctrinal texts and by Crone and Zimmermann's edition of the early Ibadi epistle of Salim ibn Dhakwan and the Sunni creedal position through al-Tahawi's creed. No encyclopedias are cited; the encyclopedia references inside the SUNY translators' footnotes are not relied on. Confidence: the two al-Tabari volumes and the al-Bukhari reports are rated high because the cited foreword pages and narrative passages were read directly for this entry (vol. 16, Editors' Foreword p. xvii, for the Camel date; vol. 17, Translator's Foreword pp. xiii-xv and p. 213, for Siffin, the arbitration, the secession, al-Nahrawan, and Ali's death); the two Sahih al-Bukhari reports were read directly in translation; the other sources were verified to exist and to treat the topic but were not read line by line, so they are rated medium. Dates are given in hijri and CE.

relations.note: The First Fitna occupies the final years of the Rashidun period (656-661), the era of the first four caliphs, and marks its close.

The killing of the third caliph Uthman in 35/656 opened the civil war; demands for retribution for his blood were the stated cause of the opposition at the Camel and of Mu'awiya's refusal of allegiance.

Ali ibn Abi Talib was caliph throughout the war, fought at the Camel, Siffin, and al-Nahrawan, and was assassinated in 40/661. He is counted by Sunnis as the fourth caliph and by Shi'is as the first imam.

The Kharijites emerged from the war as the faction that seceded from Ali after Siffin, rejecting the arbitration with the formula 'judgment belongs to God alone'; Ali fought them at al-Nahrawan, and a Kharijite killed him.

Ibadism traces its intellectual descent to the moderate wing of those who broke with Ali after the arbitration; Ibadis reject the Kharijite label and hold their own evaluation of the fitna's participants.

Shi'i tradition reads the war in light of its conviction that Ali was the Prophet's designated successor; the partisans (shi'a) of Ali in this conflict are one of the historical roots of the Shi'i identity.

Sunni tradition counts Ali as the fourth rightly guided caliph while declining to condemn the Companions who fought him, treating their conflict as a matter of ijtihad; its stance toward the fitna is one element of its self-definition.
The Murji'a are associated in the heresiographical tradition with deferring (irja') judgment on the parties to the first civil war, especially Uthman and Ali, to God.
The war is a founding episode for Shi'i doctrine of the imamate, in which Ali's authority rests on divine designation rather than on election or battlefield outcome.
The contested accession of Ali, Mu'awiya's challenge, and the arbitration raised the question of how legitimate caliphal authority is constituted, which later Sunni theory of the caliphate addressed.

The Kharijite verdict that Ali and his opponents had forfeited their standing, and the later Kharijite doctrine that grave sin makes a Muslim an unbeliever, are an early instance of the practice of declaring professing Muslims unbelievers.
Uthman's promulgation of a standard codex of the Qur'an and the destruction of variant codices are reported among the grievances raised against him by some of his opponents before his killing.
The Umayyad accession that closed the First Fitna set the stage for the confrontation in 61/680 between Mu'awiya's son and successor Yazid and Ali's son al-Husayn at Karbala.

sources.citation: Madelung, Wilferd. The Succession to Muhammad: A Study of the Early Caliphate. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1997. A detailed academic reconstruction of the succession disputes from Abu Bakr through Ali's caliphate and the first civil war, including the Camel, Siffin, the arbitration, and al-Nahrawan; the Western academic lens. Noted for arguing in defense of Ali's claim. Specific claims not page-verified for this draft.

A philological and historical study of the versions of the arbitration document agreed at Siffin; the Western academic lens. Verified to exist and to treat the arbitration; not read line by line for this draft.

sources.citation: al-Tabari, Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir. Ta'rikh al-rusul wa-l-muluk (The History of al-Tabari), Vol. 16: The Community Divided: The Caliphate of 'Ali I, A.D. 656-657/A.H. 35-36, trans. Adrian Brockett. Albany: State University of New York Press, 1997. Classical chronicle of Ali's accession and the Battle of the Camel; Editors' Foreword p. xvii gives the Camel as 10 or 15 Jumada II 36/4 or 9 December 656 and notes variant reports on whether Talha and al-Zubayr gave allegiance willingly, grudgingly, or not at all. The primary-text lens. Passages cited were read directly.

Ta'rikh al-rusul wa-l-muluk (The History of al-Tabari), Vol. 17: The First Civil War: From the Battle of Siffin to the Death of 'Ali, A.D. 656-661/A.H. 36-40, trans. G. R. Hawting. Albany: State University of New York Press, 1996. Classical chronicle, largely transmitting Abu Mikhnaf and other early Iraqi reports, of Siffin, the raising of the scriptures, the arbitration, the Kharijite secession, al-Nahrawan, and Ali's killing; Translator's Foreword pp. xiii-xv (summary of the events and their significance for Sunni, Shi'i, and Khariji self-definition) and p. 213 (variant dates of Ali's death in Ramadan 40) were read directly. The primary-text lens.

sources.citation: al-Bukhari, Muhammad ibn Isma'il (d. 256/870). al-Jami' al-Sahih (Sahih al-Bukhari), Kitab al-Salat, hadith 447, and Kitab al-Jihad wa-l-Siyar, hadith 2812 (numbering of the sunnah.com / USC-MSA reference system). The report of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Prophet said of Ammar ibn Yasir that 'the rebellious party' (al-fi'a al-baghiya) would kill him, cited by Sunni scholars in assessing the parties at Siffin; the classical Sunni primary-text lens. Both reports read directly in English translation via the fawazahmed0 hadith-api mirror (eng-bukhari edition).
